claims.text: Replacing traditional EAM references with an MLIP trained on high-temperature ab initio data will improve reference–target phase-space overlap in high-entropy alloys.
Replacing EAM references with the trained MLIP will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
The proposed method applies to multicomponent high-entropy alloys such as CoCrFeMnNi in both solid and liquid states near or above melting.
The MLIP should be trained extensively on AIMD configurations from both high-temperature liquid and solid states.
The trained MLIP should replace the EAM reference in the thermodynamic-integration framework.
Training data should span approximately 0.9–1.1 times the melting temperature, corresponding roughly to 1500–2500 K depending on the alloy.
High-dimensional descriptors can capture local environments characteristic of high-entropy alloys.
A flexible MLIP trained on diverse solid and liquid configurations will more closely reproduce the ab initio phase space.
High-entropy-alloy liquids contain many atomic configurations that must be represented by the reference potential.
Improved representation of the high-temperature potential-energy landscape will reduce structural and energetic mismatch along the thermodynamic-integration path.
Reduced structural and energetic mismatch will minimize integration error relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
The MLIP could reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by roughly a factor of two relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
The factor-of-two prediction is based on analogous elemental and binary-system studies.
The primary applicability range is alloys with five or more elements in near-equiatomic proportions.
The primary temperature range is close to or slightly above the alloy melting point.
Composition variation and anharmonic effects could alter the reduction in path mismatch.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant factor-of-two reduction, or a mismatch below 5 meV/atom, would falsify the proposed improvement.
Unfavorable deviation of MLIP-based free energies from independent ab initio benchmarks would falsify the hypothesis.
